title: One night, after the hardest years, he was taken up.
subtitle: The Night Journey as a gift after struggle

row.title: He is honored
sub: the Hearing, the Seeing was with him

then: Twelve years of calling people in Makkah, and most of its leaders still said no. Then, a year before the migration, Allah took His servant by night to Jerusalem, where {reward}he led the Prophets in prayer{/reward}, and showed him {idea}great signs of his Lord{/idea}.
now: You have been praying about the same thing for years. Nothing outside has changed. You lie awake and wonder if anyone hears. {idea}He is the Hearing, the Seeing.{/idea} The night is not proof you are forgotten. Sometimes it is where the gift arrives.
old: Long hardship means Allah has stepped back from me.
new: Allah hears and sees the long years, and He honors His servant in His own time.
try: Tonight, before sleep, say Subhan Allah slowly a few times and tell Him what you are carrying.

title: Every Book carried the same line: lean on no one but Me.
subtitle: The core of the Torah given to Musa
then: Right after the Night Journey, the surah turns to Musa, who was also a servant Allah honored. Ibn Kathir notes Allah often mentions the two Prophets and their Books together. The message given to every Prophet was the same: {idea}take no protector or helper besides Me.{/idea}
now: The job interview is tomorrow. You have checked your contacts, your CV, the person who might put in a word. All good things. But your stomach still knots, because {trap}you have quietly made them your Wakil.{/trap} Use the means. Lean on Him.
old: If I line up enough people and plans, I will be safe.
new: Plans are tools. Only Allah is the One I hand my affairs to.
try: Before your next worrying task, say Hasbiyallahu wa ni'mal Wakil, then do your part.

title: You come from the ship. Your forefather was grateful.
subtitle: Nuh as the model of a thankful servant
then: Allah addresses people as the {reward}descendants of those saved in the ship with Nuh{/reward}, as a reminder of a past rescue. Ibn Kathir explains it as: follow your father's footsteps, {idea}he was a grateful servant{/idea}. He cites the hadith that Allah is pleased when a servant praises Him for a bite of food or a drink.
now: You eat lunch at your desk, scrolling, barely tasting it. Nobody you know almost drowned this week. Yet {idea}every meal is part of a long chain of rescues{/idea} you never saw. Gratitude starts as small as saying Alhamdulillah after a glass of water.
old: Gratitude is for big moments, like surviving something.
new: A grateful servant thanks Allah for the plain cup of water too.
try: Say Alhamdulillah out loud after every meal and drink today.

title: They were told in advance where arrogance would lead.
subtitle: A warning written into their own Book
then: Allah says He had already declared it to the Children of Israel {idea}in the Book revealed to them{/idea}: they would twice spread corruption and {trap}become tyrants, extremely arrogant{/trap}. The story was told in Makkah as a lesson for everyone hearing it.
now: You know the pattern. Power at work goes to your head, you snap at the junior staff, you stop listening. Your own Book has already told you how {trap}arrogance ends{/trap}. The warning is not about someone else. It is a mirror.
old: Stories of fallen nations are about other people.
new: The warning was given in advance so I could check myself first.
try: Think of one place where you have power over someone. Be gentle there today.

title: When the first warning came true, even homes were not safe.
subtitle: The first consequence arrives as promised
then: When the first episode came, Allah sent against them {trap}people of great might{/trap} who went through their homes with no fear of anyone. Ibn Kathir says many stories were told about who they were, but he leaves them out: {idea}what the Quran says is enough.{/idea}
now: You ignored the doctor's warning for two years. Then one morning you are in the hospital corridor holding the test results. Consequences rarely knock first. {idea}A promise from Allah is fulfilled{/idea}, and the time to listen is before, not after.
old: I can keep ignoring the warning signs a while longer.
new: What Allah promised comes true, so the wise time to change is now.
try: Pick one warning sign in your life you have been ignoring and take one step on it today.

title: After the fall, Allah gave them a second chance.
subtitle: Strength returned, with wealth and children

row.title: a second chance
sub: given to see what I do

then: After the punishment, Allah {reward}gave them back the upper hand{/reward}, reinforced them with wealth and children, and made them greater in number. The recovery was from Him, and the next verse makes clear it was {idea}a test of what they would do with it{/idea}.
now: You got the job back. The marriage survived the hard year. The bank account recovered. It is easy to slide straight back into old habits once the pressure lifts. {idea}A comeback is a gift and a question{/idea} at the same time.
old: Once things are good again, the lesson is over.
new: A second chance is a fresh test of how I will live now.
try: Name one thing that recovered in your life. Write one way you will treat it better this time.

title: Every good you do lands back on you. So does every harm.
subtitle: The rule in the middle of the story
then: Between the two episodes, Allah sets down the rule: {idea}if you do good, it is for yourselves; if you do evil, it is against yourselves.{/idea} Then when the second time came, enemies were allowed to {trap}humble them and enter the Masjid{/trap} again, ruining all they took.
now: You lose your temper at your sibling in the family group chat. You tell yourself they deserved it. But you are the one who cannot sleep, the one who now avoids family dinners. {idea}Harm boomerangs.{/idea} So does kindness.
old: When I hurt someone, the damage is mostly theirs.
new: Every deed, good or bad, comes back to my own account first.
try: Do one small good deed today purely as a gift to your own soul.

title: The door of mercy stays open, even after a second fall.
subtitle: Mercy offered, and a clear warning
then: After two rounds of corruption and punishment, the verse still opens with hope: {reward}it may be that your Lord has mercy on you.{/reward} But if they returned to mischief, punishment would return. Ibn Kathir explains Hell here as {trap}a prison no one escapes{/trap}.
now: You quit the habit. Then you slipped. Then you quit again and slipped again. A voice says, why bother. The verse says {reward}mercy is still on the table{/reward}. What closes the door is not falling, it is choosing to go back and stay there.
old: I have failed too many times for Allah to forgive me.
new: Mercy is still offered. The danger is returning and not turning back.
try: Make one sincere tawbah tonight for a sin you keep repeating, and ask for strength.

title: The Quran points to the straightest way through life.
subtitle: Guidance and good news for those who act
then: After the story of a people who had a Book and drifted, Allah praises His own Book, the Quran. Ibn Kathir says it {idea}directs people to the best and clearest of ways{/idea}, and brings good news to those who believe and {reward}act according to it{/reward}.
now: You have five apps for productivity, three podcasts on how to live, and a stack of self-help books half read. You keep looking for the straight road. {idea}The most upright way is already on your shelf.{/idea} It works when you do what it says.
old: I need to find the right advice somewhere out there.
new: The Quran already points to the straightest path, if I walk it.
try: Read one page of the Quran today with its translation and pick one line to act on.

title: Ignoring the Hereafter does not cancel it.
subtitle: The other half of the Quran's message

row.title: it is not real for me
sub: what I deny cannot reach me

row.title: it is already prepared
sub: it does not wait on my belief

then: The Quran brings two kinds of news. Next to the good news for believers is a warning: those who {trap}do not believe in the Hereafter{/trap} have a painful punishment prepared on the Day of Resurrection. Makkah's leaders mocked the idea of a life after death.
now: You do not have to deny the Hereafter out loud. You can just live as if it is not coming. Weekends planned, retirement planned, {idea}nothing planned for the meeting that is certain.{/idea} The verse is a gentle shake: plan for that too.
old: I will think about the Hereafter later, when I am older.
new: The Hereafter is real whether or not I think about it, so I prepare now.
try: Add one deed to your week that you are doing only for the Hereafter.

title: In anger, we pray for harm as eagerly as for good.
subtitle: Haste and the curses we throw

row.title: haste
sub: could meet an hour of answering

then: Ibn Kathir explains that people sometimes {trap}pray against themselves, their children, or their wealth{/trap} in a moment of anger. He cites the hadith: do not pray against yourselves, it may meet an hour when Allah answers. {idea}What drives it is anxiety and haste.{/idea}
now: The kids spill juice on the laptop and the words fly out: I wish I had never... The car breaks down and you curse it. You would never say these things calmly. {idea}Hasty words can become prayers.{/idea} Pause before you speak in anger.
old: Words said in anger do not count, I did not mean them.
new: My angry words can be prayers, so I guard my tongue when I am upset.
try: Next time anger rises today, replace the curse with: Allah, make it easy.

title: Night and day are signs that let you count your life.
subtitle: Time as a gift with a rhythm
then: Allah reminds people of night and day: {idea}night to rest, day to seek a living{/idea}, and both so people know the number of days, months and years, for debts, worship and dealings. Ibn Kathir notes that {reward}if time stood still{/reward}, none of this could be known.
now: Your phone shows the date, your payday comes, the calendar reminds you of a birthday. You count time constantly but rarely notice {idea}time is counting you too{/idea}. Each sunset is one day of your life finished and recorded.
old: Days just pass. There is always tomorrow.
new: Night and day are signs given so I can measure and use my life.
try: At sunset today, stop for one minute and ask: what did I do with this day?

title: Your deeds hang on your own neck, and the book opens.
subtitle: Every act fastened to its doer
then: After time, Allah speaks of the deeds done in it. Ibn Kathir says the word means {idea}deeds that fly from a person{/idea}, good and bad, fastened to the neck, a place with no escape. Al-Hasan said: your book is open now, {reward}write what you want in it{/reward}, then it will be opened again on the Day.
now: Your phone keeps every message, every search, every photo. You know how it feels when an old message resurfaces. {idea}Your own book is open right now{/idea}, and you are the one writing it. That is frightening, and also hopeful: today's page is still blank.
old: Small things I do in private disappear.
new: Every deed stays with me, and today I still hold the pen.
try: Do one quiet good deed today that no one else will ever know about.

title: You will be handed your own record and asked to read it.
subtitle: Being your own accountant on the Day

row.title: I remember it all
sub: nothing written I did not do

then: The surah was warning the people of Makkah while there was still time. The verse before says every person's deeds are fastened to his neck. Al-Hasan explained it simply: {idea}two angels write, the book is folded at death and opened again on the Day.{/idea} Then you are told to read it yourself, and you will find it {reward}perfectly just{/reward}.
now: Your screen time report on Sunday. The bank statement at the end of the month. You never argue with those numbers, because you know they are yours. {idea}The book on that Day works the same way, only it misses nothing.{/idea} The good things you did quietly are in it too.
old: If I am ever judged, I will have a lot to explain and argue about.
new: I will not need anyone to tell me what I did. I will read it and know it is true.
try: Tonight, before sleep, read back your own day in your head. Thank Allah for one good line in it.

title: Your guidance is your gain, your straying is your loss.
subtitle: No one carries another's load, and no one is punished unwarned

row.title: guided
sub: the good comes back to you

then: Makkah had heard the warning for twelve years. Ibn Kathir explains that {idea}nobody will carry anyone else's sins{/idea}, though a person who led others astray carries his own sin and theirs too. And out of His justice, Allah {reward}does not punish anyone until a messenger has reached them{/reward}.
now: You blame your upbringing, your boss, the friend who got you into the habit. Some of that is real. But the choice you make tomorrow morning is yours. {idea}So is the good it brings you.{/idea} And if you pull someone along with you, you carry that too.
old: My mistakes are mostly the fault of the people around me.
new: What I choose lands on me, and Allah is fair enough to warn before He judges.
try: Pick one habit you usually blame on someone else. Own one small part of it today.

title: When the comfortable ones rebel, a whole town falls.
subtitle: How ease at the top can undo a community
then: Scholars read this verse in more than one way. Ibn 'Abbas said in one report that {idea}Allah commanded them to obey, but they sinned{/idea}. In another, that He let the evil ones gain power or grow in number. Either way, Ibn Kathir stresses that {trap}Allah never commands immorality{/trap}. The town falls because of what its comfortable people chose.
now: The family where the one with the most money sets the tone. The office where the senior people cut corners and everyone copies. {trap}Comfort at the top spreads fast.{/trap} If you have a bit of ease and a bit of say, your example weighs more than you think.
old: Being comfortable means things are going well.
new: Comfort is a test, and the more I have, the more others follow my lead.
try: Think of one place where people look up to you. Do one small right thing there today on purpose.

title: Many generations since Nuh rose and fell.
subtitle: Your Lord sees every sin clearly

row.title: we are special
sub: it will not happen to us

row.title: same rules
sub: no one is dearer by default

then: This was a warning to Quraysh, who were rejecting the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir paraphrases the meaning: {trap}you are not dearer to Allah than those nations were{/trap}. He also notes that Ibn 'Abbas said the ten generations between Adam and Nuh all followed Islam. And {idea}nothing people do is hidden from Him{/idea}.
now: You read about a company that collapsed, a family that broke apart, a person who lost everything. Part of you thinks, that could never be me. {idea}History is not a story about other people.{/idea} The same Lord who saw them sees your Tuesday afternoon.
old: Those stories of ruined nations are about people unlike me.
new: The same rules apply to me, and the same Lord is watching kindly and closely.
try: Next time you read bad news about someone's fall, ask what lesson it holds for your own week.

title: Want only the quick world, and you may get some of it.
subtitle: The person whose whole aim is now

row.title: some get some
sub: only what He wills, to whom He wills

then: Ibn Kathir points out a detail: {idea}not everyone who wants this world gets it{/idea}. Allah gives what He wills to whom He wills. The person who chose the passing over the lasting is left, in the Hereafter, {trap}blamed and far from mercy{/trap}.
now: The side hustle that takes every evening. The follower count you check before prayer. The promotion that has become the whole point of your life. {trap}Plenty of people chase it and still do not get it.{/trap} And the ones who do still find it ends.
old: If I work hard enough, this world will give me what I want.
new: Even the world is given, not taken, and it is a poor thing to want only that.
try: Look at your plans for this week. Add one thing that only counts for the Hereafter.

title: Effort for the Hereafter is always noticed and thanked.
subtitle: Wanting it, striving for it, believing
then: Right after the one who wants only now, the verse describes the other person. Ibn Kathir explains the three parts: {idea}wanting the Hereafter, striving for it the right way by following the Messenger ﷺ, and having faith in the heart{/idea}. Their effort {reward}is appreciated{/reward}.
now: No one at work saw you hold your tongue in that meeting. No one in the family group chat knows about the money you sent quietly. You wonder if it counted. {reward}It was noticed, and it is thanked.{/reward}
old: Small good efforts that no one sees probably do not matter much.
new: Effort made for Allah with faith is never wasted. He thanks it.
try: Do one good thing today that no one will ever know about.

title: Both seekers are given from your Lord's giving.
subtitle: No one can block what He gives
then: Having described two kinds of people, the verse says Allah gives to both. Ibn Kathir explains that {idea}He is in control of all things and is never unjust{/idea}. Qatadah and Al-Hasan said the meaning is that His gifts {reward}can never be decreased or prevented{/reward} by anyone.
now: The manager who you think holds your future. The client who might cancel. The relative who controls the family business. {idea}They are channels, not the source.{/idea} Your rent this month came from the same Lord who feeds people who never thank Him.
old: The people above me decide what I get.
new: Allah is the giver, and no one can stop what He sends.
try: Before you check your bank app today, say thank you to Allah for what is in it.

title: Look at the gaps here. The gaps there are bigger.
subtitle: Differences in this world and in the Hereafter
then: Ibn Kathir describes the differences here: {idea}some rich, some poor, some die young, some live long{/idea}. But the differences in the Hereafter are greater. He cites the Prophet ﷺ saying the people of the highest levels of Paradise {reward}will be seen like distant stars on the horizon{/reward}.
now: You scroll and see a classmate's new house, a cousin's wedding abroad, a colleague's promotion. The gap stings. {idea}That gap is small and short.{/idea} The ranks that last are being earned in ordinary moments no one posts about.
old: The differences between me and others in money and status are what really matter.
new: Worldly gaps are small next to the ranks of the Hereafter, and those are still open to me.
try: When you feel envy today, turn it into a short dua for a higher rank in Paradise.

title: Lean on another god and you are left to it.
subtitle: The loneliness of a false support

row.title: another god
sub: no power to help or harm

then: This begins a series of commands in the surah, starting with the core one. Ibn Kathir explains that {trap}Allah leaves such a person to what they worshipped, which cannot help them{/trap}. He cites the Prophet ﷺ: whoever brings his need to people alone stays in need, but {reward}whoever brings it to Allah, Allah provides for him sooner or later{/reward}.
now: When the bill comes, your first call is to a friend, a loan app, a lucky charm, a horoscope. Not wrong to ask people. But if your heart rests on them, {trap}you will feel alone when they let you down{/trap}. Turn to Allah first.
old: When I am in trouble, the right person or thing will rescue me.
new: Only Allah can truly help, and leaning elsewhere leaves me forsaken.
try: The next time you need something, make dua for it before you text anyone.

title: Worship Him alone, and not even a sigh at your parents.
subtitle: Kindness to parents placed right after worship
then: Ibn Kathir notes that {idea}worshipping Allah is tied directly to honoring parents{/idea}. Uff is the mildest word of irritation, and even that is ruled out. He cites the Prophet ﷺ saying on the minbar that a person is doomed if his parents reach old age with him and {trap}they do not become his way into Paradise{/trap}.
now: Your mother asks the same question about her phone for the fourth time. Your father tells the old story again at dinner. You feel the sigh rising, the eye roll, the sharp tone. {reward}That moment is a door to Paradise.{/reward}
old: As long as I do not yell at my parents, I am a good child.
new: Even a tired sigh matters, and a soft word to them is worship.
try: Call or visit a parent today and keep your voice gentle the whole time.

title: Lower your wing to them, and ask mercy as they raised you.
subtitle: Humility and a dua for parents

row.title: the dua
sub: My Lord, have mercy on them

row.title: now I carry them
sub: I am doing them a favor

then: The verse continues the command about parents. Ibn Kathir explains it as {idea}being humble toward them in your actions{/idea}, and saying the dua when they grow old and after they die. He cites the Prophet ﷺ telling a man who wanted to go out and fight to stay with his mother, because {reward}Paradise is at her feet{/reward}.
now: You help your father into the car at the hospital and you feel like the strong one. {idea}Remember who held your hand across the road.{/idea} The tired nights, the school fees, the meals. A short dua is the least you can give back.
old: Helping my parents now is a big favor I am doing for them.
new: I am only repaying a little of what they gave me when I was small.
try: Say this dua for your parents after one prayer today: My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me.

title: He knows what you meant, and forgives those who keep returning.
subtitle: When you slip with parents, or anyone
then: Sa'id bin Jubayr said this refers to {idea}a person who said something to his parents without meaning harm{/idea}. Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib said the returners are {reward}those who sin then repent, and sin then repent{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ would say on coming home from a journey: we have returned, repenting.
now: You snapped at your mother on the phone and felt bad all evening. Or you broke the same promise to yourself for the tenth time. {reward}He knows what was in your heart.{/reward} The door is open the eleventh time too.
old: If I keep making the same mistake, my repentance must be fake.
new: Allah knows my heart, and keeps forgiving the one who keeps coming back.
try: Think of the last harsh word you said. Say astaghfirullah, then send that person a kind message.

title: Give relatives, the poor, and the traveler their right. Do not squander.
subtitle: Spending that is owed, and spending that is wasted
then: After parents come relatives. Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ: {reward}whoever wants more provision and a longer life, let him keep ties of kinship{/reward}. On waste, Mujahid said that {trap}spending a little on the wrong thing is waste{/trap}, while spending all on right things is not.
now: Payday arrives. Delivery apps, a new gadget, subscriptions you forgot about. Then your cousin messages asking for help with school fees and you feel stretched. {idea}The cousin was owed first.{/idea}
old: Helping relatives is generous of me when I have extra.
new: My relatives and the needy have a right in my money, and waste takes from them.
try: Cancel one subscription you do not use and give that amount to a relative or someone in need.

title: Wasters are brothers of the devils.
subtitle: Waste as a form of ingratitude
then: Ibn Kathir says wasters share traits with the devils: {trap}extravagance, foolishness, disobeying Allah{/trap}. Shaytan is called ungrateful because {idea}he denied Allah's blessings and turned them to disobedience{/idea}. Waste is a blessing used the wrong way.
now: Half the food from the party in the bin. The phone replaced while the old one still works fine. The impulse buy at midnight. {idea}Each one was a gift first.{/idea} Using it carelessly is a quiet way of not saying thank you.
old: Wasting a bit of money or food is not a big deal.
new: Waste is ingratitude for a gift, and gratitude means using it well.
try: Before you throw any food away today, see if it can be eaten, saved, or given.

title: When you have nothing to give, give a gentle word.
subtitle: Saying no without breaking a heart

row.title: an easy, kind reply
sub: when I have, I will give

then: The verses before command giving to relatives, the poor and travelers. This one covers the moment {idea}you have nothing to give and must turn them away{/idea}. Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan and others said the gentle word means {reward}a kind promise{/reward} that you will help when Allah gives you something.
now: A cousin asks for money in a voice note. Your account is empty until the end of the month. The easy move is to leave it on read. {trap}Silence feels like rejection.{/trap} {reward}A warm reply costs nothing.{/reward}
old: If I cannot give anything, there is nothing I owe the person asking.
new: Even with empty hands, I owe them kindness and a hopeful word.
try: Reply today to one request you have been avoiding, kindly, even if the answer is not yet.

title: Not a hand chained shut, not a hand thrown wide open.
subtitle: The middle path in spending
then: Ibn Kathir says the verse {idea}condemns stinginess and forbids extravagance{/idea}. The miser is blamed and people stop relying on him. The one who spends beyond his means ends up with nothing, worn out. He cites the Prophet ﷺ: {reward}wealth never decreases because of charity{/reward}.
now: Some people never pick up the bill, never chip in for the gift. Others say yes to every request, then borrow to pay rent. {idea}Both hands get tired.{/idea} A steady giving habit, sized to your income, lasts.
old: Being generous means giving whenever I am asked, whatever it costs.
new: Generosity has a shape: open, but not so open that I break.
try: Set a small fixed amount you will give every week, one you can keep up.

title: He widens provision for some and tightens it for others.
subtitle: Who decides rich and poor, and why
then: Right after the command to spend wisely, the verse reminds who gives. Ibn Kathir says {idea}Allah makes rich and poor by His wisdom{/idea}, knowing who is suited to each. He adds that {trap}wealth can carry someone away to ruin, and poverty can be a punishment{/trap}, and asks Allah's protection from both.
now: Your friend's business takes off. Yours struggles even though you work longer hours. You start to wonder if Allah is pleased with them and not with you. {idea}The amount is not the verdict.{/idea} What you do with it is.
old: How much money I have shows how Allah sees me.
new: Allah gives more or less with wisdom, and each amount is a test.
try: Whatever your balance today, say alhamdulillah and ask Allah to protect you from the test in it.

title: We provide for them and for you.
subtitle: Fear of poverty must never cost a child
then: In pre-Islamic Arabia some people killed their daughters for fear of becoming poorer. Ibn Kathir notes that {reward}the children's provision is mentioned first here{/reward}, and that Allah is more compassionate to His servants than a father to his child. He calls the act {trap}a major sin{/trap}.
now: You do the sums at the kitchen table. School fees, rent, another baby on the way. The fear grips your chest. {reward}The verse speaks straight to that fear.{/reward} Plan wisely, but remember who has always fed this house.
old: My children's future depends entirely on how much I can earn.
new: Allah provides for my children before He provides for me.
try: When money worry about your family rises today, say: Allah provides for them and for me.

title: Do not even go near it.
subtitle: Staying far from the road to zina
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah forbids zina and {idea}everything that leads to it{/idea}. He cites a young man who asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission. The people scolded him, but the Prophet ﷺ called him close and asked if he would like it for his mother, his daughter, his sister. Then he put his hand on him and {reward}prayed for his heart to be purified{/reward}.
now: It starts small. A late night message that gets a bit too personal. The app you open when you are lonely. {trap}No one plans the fall.{/trap} The verse does not say do not do it. It says do not walk toward it.
old: I can handle getting close as long as I do not cross the final line.
new: The safe place is far from the line, not right next to it.
try: Identify one door that leads you toward temptation and close it today, a chat, an app, a habit.

title: A life Allah made sacred, and justice without excess.
subtitle: The weight of one soul
then: Ibn Kathir cites a narration that {idea}the end of the world is less serious to Allah than the killing of a Muslim{/idea}. The heir of a wronged person is given authority, and may also forgive. But {trap}he must not go beyond limits{/trap}, such as taking revenge on people other than the one who did it.
now: Someone wrongs your brother, and the family group chat fills with rage. Everyone wants to hit back at the whole other family. {trap}Anger wants more than justice.{/trap} The verse puts a limit on that.
old: When I am wronged, I am free to get back at them however I like.
new: Even rightful anger has limits, and forgiving is always an option.
try: Think of someone who wronged you. Make sure you are not punishing someone else for it.

title: Guard the orphan's money, and keep every promise.
subtitle: Things trusted to you will be asked about
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the orphan's wealth must only be handled {idea}in a proper way{/idea}, until he is grown. He cites the Prophet ﷺ telling Abu Dharr not to take charge of an orphan's property, because {trap}it is a heavy trust{/trap}. Every promise you make to people {idea}will be asked about{/idea}.
now: You told your colleague you would cover for her shift. You promised your son you would come to his match. You are holding a friend's money for safekeeping. {idea}Each one is a small trust.{/idea} Keeping it is worship.
old: A promise is fine to drop if something better comes up.
new: Every promise I make will be asked about, so I keep it or I do not make it.
try: Look back over the last week for one promise you have not yet kept. Keep it today.

title: Give full measure and weigh with an honest scale.
subtitle: Honesty in what you hand over
then: Ibn Kathir explains the balance must be {idea}straight, not distorted{/idea}. Qatadah said this is better in reward and in outcome. Ibn 'Abbas used to say: {trap}you are trusted with two things that destroyed the people before you, weights and measures{/trap}.
now: The timesheet with an extra half hour. The product photo that hides the flaw. The rounding up on the expense claim. {trap}Small, quiet, everyday.{/trap} {reward}Giving people exactly what they paid for is better for you in the end.{/reward}
old: Shaving a little off is normal business, everyone does it.
new: Fair measure is good for me now and better for me later.
try: Check one thing you hand over today, hours, work, change, and make sure it is full.

title: Do not follow what you do not know.
subtitle: Hearing, sight and heart will be questioned
then: Qatadah explained: {idea}do not say I saw when you did not see, or I heard when you did not hear{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says Allah forbids speaking on suspicion. He cites the narration that {trap}it is an evil habit for a man to keep saying they claimed{/trap}.
now: A screenshot lands in the family chat about someone you know. You are about to forward it. You are not sure it is true. {trap}Forwarding is saying it yourself.{/trap} Your thumb will be asked about it.
old: If I just pass something on, I am not responsible for whether it is true.
new: What I repeat is mine, and I will be asked how I knew it.
try: Before you share any news today, ask yourself: do I actually know this is true?

title: You cannot split the earth or rise as tall as mountains.
subtitle: Arrogance meets reality
then: The surah's list of commands turns to how a person walks. Ibn Kathir says this forbids {trap}walking boastfully, like arrogant oppressors{/trap}. He mentions Qarun, who came out to his people in his finery, and {trap}the earth swallowed him and his house{/trap}.
now: The new car, the new title on your email signature, the way you walk into the room after the promotion. {idea}Stand next to a mountain and see.{/idea} The earth under your feet was here long before you and will be here after.
old: My success gives me the right to carry myself above others.
new: Next to the earth and the mountains, I am small, and that is freeing.
try: Go outside and look at the sky or a hill for one minute. Feel your real size.

title: All of these, the evil of them, your Lord hates.
subtitle: A pause after the list of commands
then: Ibn Kathir explains that this verse {idea}gathers everything mentioned from 17:23 up to here{/idea}: worship, parents, kin, waste, children, zina, killing, orphans, promises, honest scales, speaking without knowledge, and arrogance. Read one way, {trap}all of it is evil deeds{/trap}. Read the other, it means the bad among them is disliked by Allah.
now: Think of these verses as a checklist on your fridge. Parents. Relatives. Spending. Honesty. Rumors. Pride. {idea}It is a whole picture of a good life.{/idea} You do not have to fix all of it this week.
old: Religious rules are just a list of things I am not allowed to do.
new: These commands describe a decent life, and what they forbid is what harms it.
try: Read 17:23 to 17:38 once more and pick the one line you most need right now.

title: This is wisdom from your Lord. Begin and end with tawhid.
subtitle: The list closes where it opened
then: Ibn Kathir explains that everything commanded is {reward}good manners{/reward} and everything forbidden is an evil quality, revealed to the Prophet ﷺ so he could teach the people. The warning against shirk returns at the end, {trap}blamed by one's own self, by Allah and by people{/trap}. It is addressed to the community through the Prophet ﷺ.
now: You can be kind, honest and generous for many reasons. Reputation. Habit. Upbringing. {idea}The verse ties all of it back to one root.{/idea} When you do good for Allah, it holds even on the days no one is watching.
old: Being a good person has nothing to do with what I believe about God.
new: Good manners are wisdom from Allah, and they stand firmest on believing in Him alone.
try: Before one kind act today, quietly make the intention that it is for Allah.

title: Sons for you, and daughters for Him? A grave thing to say.
subtitle: Exposing an unfair claim about Allah
then: The idolaters of Makkah claimed the angels were daughters of Allah and worshipped them. Ibn Kathir says {trap}they were wrong on three counts{/trap}: giving Allah children, making them female, and worshipping them. They gave Allah what they disliked for themselves. {idea}The angels are servants of the Most Merciful.{/idea}
now: Notice how easy it is to keep the best for yourself and hand Allah the leftovers. The best hours for work, the tired minutes for prayer. {idea}The verse asks what you are giving Him.{/idea}
old: Allah gets whatever time and energy I have left over.
new: Allah deserves the best of me, not what I would not want for myself.
try: Give one prayer today your fresh attention, before the phone, not after.

title: Explained in many ways, yet some only run further.
subtitle: The same reminder can soften or harden
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah set out His warnings in many forms so people would {reward}remember the proof and be held back from shirk and wrongdoing{/reward}. But {trap}the wrongdoers among them only went further from the truth{/trap}.
now: A friend sends you a reminder and you feel annoyed, not grateful. The khutbah topic hits too close and you tune out. {trap}That pull away is worth noticing.{/trap} The same words that push you off can bring you back if you stay.
old: If a reminder makes me uncomfortable, it is badly delivered.
new: When I want to turn away from a reminder, that is the moment to listen harder.
try: Think of the last reminder that annoyed you. Reread it today with an open heart.

title: Even other gods, if they existed, would be seeking Him.
subtitle: No need for a middleman to reach Allah
then: The idolaters of Makkah worshipped others so these would bring them closer to Allah and speak for them. The reply: {idea}if such gods existed, they would themselves be seeking a way to Him{/idea}. So worship Him alone. Ibn Kathir notes that {trap}He does not accept intermediaries in worship{/trap} and forbade it through all His messengers.
now: You feel too far gone to make dua yourself. You ask someone more pious to pray for you instead and never pray yourself. {idea}There is no queue and no receptionist.{/idea} Raise your hands. He hears you directly.
old: I need someone holier than me to get my prayers through.
new: Allah is reachable directly, by me, right now.
try: Make one dua today in your own words, in your own language, with no one in between.

title: Glorified and far above what they claim.
subtitle: A moment of tasbih in the middle of the argument
then: After answering the claim of other gods, the Quran pauses to glorify Allah. Ibn Kathir describes Him as {idea}the One, the Self-Sufficient Master whom all creatures need{/idea}. He begets not, nor was He begotten, and {idea}there is none comparable to Him{/idea}.
now: You have just finished an argument in your head about why you are right. Or you scrolled past a post mocking faith and felt your chest tighten. {idea}Stop and say subhanallah.{/idea} His greatness does not depend on winning anything.
old: When someone says something wrong about Allah, I must defend Him angrily.
new: Allah is far above any claim, and my first response can be to glorify Him.
try: Say subhanahu wa ta'ala slowly three times when you next hear something careless about Allah.

title: Everything is glorifying Him. You just cannot hear it.
subtitle: Creation's hidden tasbih, and His patience

row.title: only I forget
sub: and He is patient with me

then: Ibn Kathir explains that {idea}every creature, animal, plant and even lifeless things, glorifies Allah{/idea} in a way not like human speech. Ibn Mas'ud said: we used to hear the food glorifying Allah as it was eaten. And He is {reward}Forbearing and Forgiving{/reward}, giving people time to return.
now: The birds outside your window at dawn. The rain on the bus stop roof. The tree you walk past every day without looking. {idea}All of it is busy with praise.{/idea} The only one scrolling in silence might be you.
old: Nature is just background, it does not mean anything.
new: Everything around me is praising Allah, and I am invited to join.
try: On your next walk, say subhanallah each time you notice a tree, a bird, or the sky.

title: An invisible veil falls between the reciter and the unwilling.
subtitle: When the Quran is heard but not received
then: Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said the veil is {trap}coverings over their hearts{/trap}. Asma' bint Abi Bakr narrated that when Umm Jamil came with a stone pestle looking for the Prophet ﷺ, he recited this verse and {reward}she stood by Abu Bakr without seeing him{/reward}.
now: You play Quran in the car every morning. It is just sound now, like the radio. {trap}Words can pass over a heart without landing.{/trap} The veil is not always somebody else's.
old: If I hear the Quran often enough, it will reach me automatically.
new: The Quran reaches an open heart, so I need to listen with mine.
try: Listen to one short surah today with nothing else going on, and focus on its meaning.

title: When He alone is mentioned, they turn their backs.
subtitle: Discomfort with pure tawhid
then: Ibn Kathir says when the Prophet ﷺ declared Allah to be One in his recitation, {trap}they turned away in strong dislike{/trap}. Qatadah said the idolaters found La ilaha illallah intolerable, but {reward}Allah insisted on supporting it until it prevailed{/reward}.
now: Talking about religion is fine at dinner, as long as it stays general. When it gets to my life belongs to Allah alone, people change the subject. {idea}Notice if you do too.{/idea} That is the part worth staying with.
old: A bit of faith is nice, but too much focus on Allah alone is extreme.
new: Allah alone is the heart of it, and I should not flinch from that.
try: Say La ilaha illallah slowly 33 times today, thinking of one thing it means for you.

title: They listened in secret, then called him bewitched.
subtitle: Hearing the truth and still refusing it
then: Ibn Ishaq narrated that Abu Sufyan, Abu Jahl and Al-Akhnas each secretly listened to the Prophet ﷺ praying at night, {idea}three nights in a row{/idea}. Later Abu Jahl admitted the real reason: his clan had competed with Banu 'Abd Manaf in honor, and {trap}now they had a prophet, so we will never believe{/trap}.
now: You know your colleague's idea is the best one. But it is theirs, and you have been competing all year. So you find something to criticize. {trap}Rivalry can make a person argue against what they know is true.{/trap}
old: I reject things because they are wrong, not because of who said them.
new: Sometimes I resist truth because of pride, and I need to catch it.
try: Today, openly agree with one good idea from someone you usually compete with.

title: See the labels they invent for you. They lose the way.
subtitle: Name-calling as a way to avoid the message
then: Ibn Kathir lists the names they tried on the Prophet ﷺ: {trap}poet, soothsayer, crazy, sorcerer, bewitched{/trap}. They kept changing the label. The verse says they went astray, and {trap}could not find a way to the truth{/trap}.
now: Someone gives you honest advice and you file them under judgmental, or extreme, or too religious. Then you do not have to think about what they said. {idea}A label is an easy exit.{/idea}
old: Once I know what type of person someone is, I can ignore what they say.
new: Labeling the speaker is often a way of dodging the message.
try: Think of one piece of advice you dismissed because of who said it. Reconsider just the words.

title: Bones and dust, made new again?
subtitle: The old doubt about resurrection
then: The people of Makkah thought the resurrection very unlikely. Mujahid said fragments means earth, and Ibn 'Abbas said dust. They asked {trap}after we have crumbled and been forgotten, will we really be raised?{/trap} The next verses give the answer.
now: You stand at a grave after the burial and look at the soil. It feels so final. A quiet doubt creeps in: is that really it? {idea}The Quran heard that question long ago and did not mock it.{/idea} It answered.
old: Once someone is dust, it is hard to imagine anything after.
new: Becoming dust is no obstacle to the One who made me from nothing.
try: Visit a grave or remember someone who passed, and say a dua for them and for your own return.

title: Be stone or iron if you like.
subtitle: Harder materials, same answer
then: The reply to their doubt is a challenge. Ibn Kathir says stone and iron are {idea}harder to restore than bones and fragments{/idea}. Become whatever you want, Allah will still bring you back, because {idea}nothing can stop Him when He wills a thing{/idea}.
now: You think some part of your life is set in stone. The hard heart. The broken marriage. The habit of twenty years. {reward}If He can raise iron to life, He can soften this.{/reward}
old: Some things in me are too hard to ever change.
new: Nothing is too hard for Allah to remake, including me.
try: Name one thing in your life you think is set in stone. Ask Allah to change it.

title: Who will bring us back? The One who made you first.
subtitle: The answer, the mocking nod, and maybe soon
then: Ibn Kathir explains that He who created you {idea}when you were nothing{/idea} can create you anew. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said shaking their heads was {trap}a gesture of mockery{/trap}. The answer to when is a warning: {idea}perhaps it is near{/idea}.
now: Your phone shows your baby photos. Once you were not even that. {idea}You were made from nothing once already.{/idea} And the when question? No one gets a date. That is why today matters.
old: The Day of Judgment is so far away that I do not need to think about it.
new: The One who made me once will make me again, and it may be nearer than I think.
try: Look at an old photo of yourself as a baby and remember who brought you into being.

title: Called out, you will rise praising, and life will feel short.
subtitle: How long this world will seem afterwards
then: Ibn Kathir explains it will be {idea}one definitive command{/idea}, and people will come out from the earth in response. Rising from their graves, {trap}they will think they stayed in this world only a little{/trap}. He cites verses where people say a day, or part of a day.
now: Remember how fast your school years went. The last decade. The last Ramadan. {idea}Life on that Day will feel shorter than any of those.{/idea} The things you are putting off for later have less later than you think.
old: I have a long life ahead, there is plenty of time to get serious.
new: Life will feel like a short afternoon, so the time to begin is now.
try: Do today one good thing you have been saving for someday.

title: Say the best words. Shaytan works through the gaps.
subtitle: Speech among believers
then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to instruct the believers to {idea}speak to one another with the best and politest words{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains that otherwise {trap}Shaytan sows discord, and words lead to actions and fights{/trap}. He cites the Prophet ﷺ forbidding anyone to point a weapon at his brother even in jest.
now: The family group chat at 11pm. A sarcastic reply. A voice note with an edge. By morning two siblings are not speaking. {trap}It started with one word.{/trap} {idea}The best word could have ended it.{/idea}
old: I just say what I think, people should not be so sensitive.
new: My words open or close the door for Shaytan, so I choose the best ones.
try: Before sending one message today, reread it and change one word to a kinder one.

title: Your Lord knows you best. You were not sent as their keeper.
subtitle: Leaving the outcome to Allah
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah {idea}knows best who deserves to be guided{/idea}, and His mercy includes helping a person to obey Him. The Prophet ﷺ was told {reward}We have sent you as a warner{/reward}, not as a guardian over them.
now: Your brother has stopped praying. You have sent him reminders, lectures, links. You are exhausted and angry. {idea}You are not his keeper.{/idea} Speak kindly, pray for him, and leave the rest to the One who knows his heart.
old: If the people I love do not change, I have failed.
new: My job is to speak well and pray. Guidance is Allah's.
try: Make a sincere dua today for one person you have been trying to change.

title: He knows everyone in heaven and earth, and ranked the prophets.
subtitle: Preference is His choice, not our whims

row.title: your Lord
sub: knows all in heaven and earth

then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah knows each person's level of obedience. He preferred some prophets over others, but the hadith forbidding preference refers to {trap}preference based on whims and sectarian feeling{/trap}. Dawud was honored with the Zabur, which {reward}was made so easy for him he could finish it while his mount was being saddled{/reward}.
now: Online, people argue about which scholar or which group is best, and it turns into tribal fights. {trap}Ranking out of loyalty.{/trap} {idea}Leave the ranking to Allah, and learn from all who carried His message.{/idea}
old: My group and my teachers are simply better than the rest.
new: Allah knows who is above whom, and my job is to learn, not to take sides.
try: Learn one thing today about a prophet you know little about, like Dawud.

title: Call on them. They cannot lift your hardship, or even shift it.
subtitle: Testing what you rely on
then: The Prophet ﷺ was told to challenge the idolaters directly: go ahead and call on them. Ibn Kathir says {trap}they have no power at all{/trap} to remove a hardship, or even to pass it onto someone else. {idea}Only Allah can do that{/idea}, the One who creates and commands.
now: The test results come back bad. You refresh the forum, call the specialist, read every article at 2am. All of that is fine. {idea}But none of it can lift this.{/idea} Make sure your first and last call is to Him.
old: The right expert or connection can fix my problem.
new: People are means, but only Allah can remove or even shift a hardship.
try: Before your next appointment or call about a problem, make dua for it first.

title: The ones they worship are themselves racing to get closer to Allah.
subtitle: Hope and fear, the two wings of worship
then: Ibn 'Abbas said the idolaters worshipped angels and others who {idea}were themselves calling on Allah{/idea}. Ibn Mas'ud reported that some jinn who were worshipped later became Muslims. Ibn Kathir adds that {reward}worship is complete only with fear and hope together{/reward}: fear holds you back from sin, hope moves you to do good.
now: Some days you feel so sure of Allah's mercy you get careless. Other days you feel so afraid you give up. {idea}Both are a wing missing.{/idea} The righteous ones you admire most fly with both.
old: Either Allah forgives everything, or I am too far gone.
new: I hope for His mercy and fear His punishment, and that balance keeps me going.
try: Make one dua for mercy and one for protection from punishment after your next prayer.

title: Every wrongdoing town's end is already written.
subtitle: Nothing is outside His record
then: Ibn Kathir explains that it is written in the Preserved Tablet that towns will meet ruin or hardship before the Day of Resurrection {trap}because of their sins{/trap}. He cites the verse about past nations: {idea}We did not wrong them, they wronged themselves{/idea}.
now: Nothing in this world is permanent, not your city, not your company, not your street. {idea}What lasts is what you did in it.{/idea} When you see a place decline, ask what you are building in your own corner.
old: The places and systems around me will always be there.
new: Every place has a written end, so I should invest in what lasts.
try: Do one good deed today for your neighborhood, something small that helps someone nearby.

title: Signs on demand were held back, out of mercy.
subtitle: Why the miracle they asked for did not come
then: Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ to turn the hill of As-Safa into gold. Ibn 'Abbas narrated that Allah gave him a choice: the sign, with punishment if they still disbelieved, or {reward}the gates of repentance and mercy{/reward}. He chose mercy. The earlier peoples, like Thamud with the she-camel, {trap}had denied their signs and been destroyed{/trap}.
now: You tell yourself: if Allah just showed me something clear, I would change. But plenty of people saw and did not. {reward}The time you have right now is the mercy.{/reward} An eclipse, a tremor, a scare at the doctor are reminders too.
old: If I got a clear sign, I would finally get serious.
new: The extra time I have been given is itself a mercy and a sign.
try: Next time something frightens you, a storm or bad news, stop and make istighfar.

title: The Night Journey vision and the tree of Zaqqum were tests.
subtitle: What sorted the believers from the doubters

key.label: When it is hard to grasp

then: Ibn 'Abbas said the vision was {idea}what the Prophet ﷺ saw with his own eyes on the Night Journey{/idea}. Ibn Kathir notes some people left Islam because their minds could not grasp it, while {reward}it strengthened the faith of others{/reward}. Abu Jahl mocked the tree of Zaqqum by eating dates and butter. And Allah had told the Prophet ﷺ He had encompassed the people, meaning He would protect him.
now: You hit a part of the faith that your mind struggles with. The unseen. Something that does not fit your science class. {idea}That moment is a test.{/idea} Some people walk away. Others sit with it and find their trust deepens.
old: If I cannot fully understand something in my faith, I should doubt it.
new: What my mind cannot fully grasp can still be true, and trusting it is a test.
try: Write down one thing in faith that puzzles you. Ask a teacher, and ask Allah for understanding.

title: All bowed to Adam except Iblis, who scorned the clay.
subtitle: The oldest arrogance
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {trap}an ancient hatred{/trap}, from the moment Adam was created. Iblis refused out of arrogance and said, with contempt, shall I bow to one made of clay? In another verse he says {trap}I am better than him{/trap}.
now: You look at someone and decide in a second you are better: your degree, your family, your accent, your neighborhood. {trap}That I am better than him is the first sin ever recorded against a human.{/trap}
old: Some people are simply beneath me because of where they come from.
new: Thinking I am better by birth is the voice of Iblis, not of faith.
try: Today, go out of your way to show respect to someone you tend to look down on.

title: Give me time, said Iblis, and I will mislead his children.
subtitle: The enemy's stated plan
then: Iblis spoke to his Lord with insolence, and {reward}the Lord bore it patiently{/reward}. Ibn 'Abbas said he meant: I will dominate his offspring. Mujahid said: I will surround them. Ibn Zayd: {trap}I will lead them astray, all but a few{/trap}.
now: Your enemy told everyone his plan in advance. Surround you. Wear you down. Keep you scrolling, delaying, doubting. {idea}Knowing the plan is half the defense.{/idea} Aim to be in the few.
old: I am not really a target, I am just an ordinary person.
new: Shaytan has openly declared his plan against me, so I stay alert.
try: Say a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim the next time you feel the pull to delay a prayer.

title: Go, then. Whoever follows you shares your end.
subtitle: The respite and the warning
then: Allah granted Iblis respite until the appointed Day, and warned him and {trap}whoever of Adam's children follows him{/trap}. Qatadah said the recompense will be abundant and not decreased. The key word is follows.
now: Shaytan can whisper, but he cannot drag. Every time you open that app, scroll that feed, or say that word, {idea}you are the one taking the step{/idea}. The good news: you can also stop following.
old: When I give in to temptation, it is the devil's fault.
new: He only invites, and following him is my choice to make or refuse.
try: Identify one whisper you followed this week. Decide today to refuse it next time.

title: His voice, his forces, his share, his promises: all deceit.
subtitle: Shaytan's toolkit
then: Ibn 'Abbas said his voice is {trap}every caller who calls people to disobey Allah{/trap}. His share in wealth is money spent in disobedience. Ibn Kathir says {idea}anything in which a person obeys Shaytan, he is sharing in it{/idea}. On the Day, Iblis himself will admit: I promised you, but I betrayed you.
now: The ad that says you deserve it. The friend who says just this once. The voice that says you will repent later. {trap}A promise of later is one of his favorites.{/trap} Notice how many of his promises are about tomorrow.
old: I will enjoy this now and fix things later.
new: Shaytan's promises always break, especially the one about later.
try: Say bismillah before you spend money today, and see if it changes what you buy.

title: Over My servants you have no authority.
subtitle: The protection of being Allah's servant
then: After listing Shaytan's whole toolkit, the passage ends with reassurance. Ibn Kathir says {reward}Allah supports His believing servants and guards them{/reward} against the accursed one. He is enough as a Protector, Supporter and Helper.
now: After a bad week of slipping, it can feel like the whispers always win. {reward}They do not get the last word.{/reward} The closer you hold to being His servant, prayer, dhikr, honest repentance, the less grip they have.
old: Shaytan is too strong, I will always lose to him.
new: As Allah's servant, I am under His guard, and Shaytan cannot own me.
try: Read Ayat al-Kursi before you sleep tonight and rest in His protection.

title: Your Lord drives the ship so you can seek His bounty.
subtitle: Mercy in ordinary travel and trade
then: After the warnings about Shaytan, the surah turns to Allah's kindness. Ibn Kathir says He made ships {idea}easy to use for trade between one region and another{/idea}. He does this {reward}out of His grace and mercy{/reward}.
now: The cargo ship that brought your phone. The bus you take to work. The delivery van with your groceries. {reward}A whole chain of travel brings your daily bread.{/reward} Every trip you take for your living is held up by His mercy.
old: Getting to work and earning a living is just logistics.
new: Every journey that brings me provision is a mercy from my Lord.
try: Say the travel dua, subhanalladhi sakhkhara lana hadha, on your next commute.

title: In the storm, only He remains. On land, you forget.
subtitle: Sincere in danger, careless in safety
then: 'Ikrimah bin Abi Jahl fled Makkah after its conquest and took a boat toward Ethiopia. A storm hit and the sailors said only Allah can save you. He thought: {idea}if only Allah helps at sea, only Allah helps on land{/idea}. He promised to go to the Prophet ﷺ if he survived, and he did, {reward}and became a good Muslim{/reward}.
now: The turbulence on the flight. The night in the hospital corridor. You prayed like never before. Then it passed, and within a week you were back to skipping Fajr. {idea}Be like 'Ikrimah: keep the promise you made in the storm.{/idea}
old: I turn to Allah seriously when things get really bad.
new: The Allah I called in the storm is the same Allah on calm days.
try: Remember one promise you made to Allah in a hard moment. Keep part of it today.

title: Is dry land really safer?
subtitle: The false feeling of security
then: This speaks to the person who turned away once the boat reached land. Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}do you think dry land makes you safe from Him?{/trap} Mujahid said Hasib is rain that carries stones, like what came on the people of Lut, except his family, whom {reward}Allah saved before dawn{/reward}.
now: The scare is over, the scan was clear, the job is safe. You exhale and go back to normal. {idea}Your safety today is as much a gift as your rescue was.{/idea} It is not a reason to forget Him.
old: Once the danger has passed, I am safe on my own.
new: I am never safe by myself. Every calm day is held up by Allah.
try: On a normal, calm day this week, thank Allah for one danger you are not in.

title: Or He could send you back to sea a second time.
subtitle: The storm you survived can return

row.title: no avenger
sub: no one to take your side

then: Ibn Kathir explains this is addressed to those who {trap}turn away after acknowledging Allah's Oneness at sea{/trap}. Ibn 'Abbas said the Qasif is the sea wind that breaks vessels. And {trap}no one will come to avenge them{/trap} against Allah.
now: You got through the layoff, the illness, the family crisis. Life can bring the same storm back. {idea}The rescue was not a pass.{/idea} It was a chance to come back to Him for good, while the weather is calm.
old: I already went through my hard times, so I am done with that.
new: Being rescued is a second chance, and the wise use it before the next storm.
try: Write down one way you changed after a hard time. Check that you are still doing it.

title: We have honored the children of Adam.
subtitle: Your dignity is a gift, not an achievement
then: Ibn Kathir describes the honor: {reward}created in the best form, walking upright, eating with the hand{/reward}, given hearing, sight and a heart to tell what helps from what harms. Carried on animals and ships, fed with every kind of good food, and dressed in clothes of every color.
now: A bad day at work. A breakup. A rejection email. You feel worthless. {reward}Before any of that, Allah honored you.{/reward} And every person you pass on the street, the cleaner, the stranger, the one you disagree with, carries that same honor.
old: My worth goes up and down with how my life is going.
new: Allah gave me dignity as a child of Adam, and no bad day can take it.
try: Treat one person today, a cleaner, a driver, a cashier, with the honor Allah gave them.

title: Each people called with its record. Right-hand readers read with joy.
subtitle: Not wronged by a date-seed's thread
then: Scholars differed on the word Imam here. Ibn Kathir prefers the view of Ibn 'Abbas: {idea}it is the record of deeds{/idea}. Those given it in the right hand {reward}will read it out of happiness{/reward}. The Fatil is the tiny thread in the groove of a date seed, and {idea}not even that much injustice will be done{/idea}.
now: You picture the Day and only imagine dread. But there is another scene: someone so happy with their book they want everyone to read it. {reward}That can be you.{/reward} Every small good deed this week is a line you would love to read out.
old: Thinking about my record on that Day can only bring me fear.
new: My record can be something I read with joy, and I am writing it now.
try: Do one good deed today and picture yourself happily reading it on that Day.

title: Blind here, blind there.
subtitle: Seeing the signs while you still can
then: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said this is about {idea}this worldly life{/idea}. Blind means {trap}blind to the signs and proofs of Allah{/trap}. Whoever lives that way stays that way in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir ends by seeking refuge with Allah from it.
now: You walk past a sunset staring at your phone. You get well after an illness and do not even say alhamdulillah. {idea}Seeing is a habit you build here.{/idea} The eyes you train now are the eyes you carry there.
old: I will understand everything clearly once I die.
new: The sight I build now is the sight I will have later.
try: Look for one sign of Allah today, in nature, in your body, in an answered prayer, and name it.

title: They almost pulled him away from the revelation.
subtitle: The pressure to soften the message
then: This passage speaks of the opponents' attempts to sway the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir says it shows how {reward}Allah supported His Prophet ﷺ, protected him, and kept him safe from the plots of the wicked{/reward}. He would not leave him to any of His creation.
now: Your friends say you would fit in better if you relaxed a bit. Your colleagues joke about the prayer break. {trap}The offer is always friendship in exchange for a little less.{/trap} Real friends do not ask you to change what Allah said.
old: To be accepted, I need to bend my values a little.
new: Friendship bought by giving up the truth is not worth having.
try: Next time you feel pressure to hide your faith, do one small thing openly, calmly.

title: Had We not made you firm, you might have leaned a little.
subtitle: Steadiness is a gift from Allah
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah {reward}is the One who took care of His Prophet ﷺ and helped him{/reward}, his Helper, Supporter and Protector. The verse shows that {idea}even steadiness comes from Allah{/idea}. If the Prophet ﷺ was told this, how much more do we need it.
now: You feel proud that you did not give in this time. You stayed home from that party, you closed that tab. {idea}That strength was given to you.{/idea} Thank Him for it, and ask Him again tomorrow.
old: I stay on track because I am disciplined.
new: Allah keeps me firm, so I thank Him and keep asking.
try: After your next prayer, ask Allah in your own words to keep your heart firm on His way.

title: For the one who knows most, the stakes are double.
subtitle: Responsibility grows with closeness
then: The verse continues the address to the Prophet ﷺ, the one Allah protected. It is a sober reminder that {idea}the one given the most is held to the highest standard{/idea}, and that {trap}no one could help against Allah{/trap}. Ibn Kathir stresses that Allah kept him safe and firm.
now: You know more about your deen than you did five years ago. You teach your kids, you share reminders. {idea}That knowledge raises the bar for you.{/idea} Not to scare you. To remind you to live what you know.
old: The more I know, the safer I am.
new: The more I know, the more I am responsible to live by it.
try: Pick one thing you often tell others to do. Do it yourself today.

title: They nearly drove him out, but they would not last long after.
subtitle: Pushing out the messenger has a cost

row.conn: a year and a half later

then: Ibn Kathir says this was revealed about Quraysh, who {trap}wanted to expel the Messenger of Allah ﷺ{/trap}. After the persecution forced him to migrate, only about a year and a half later {idea}Allah brought them together at Badr without any appointment{/idea}, and the Prophet ﷺ prevailed.
now: You push the reminders out of your life. Unfollow the friend who posts about prayer. Stop going to the masjid because it makes you feel guilty. {trap}It feels like relief.{/trap} But pushing out what is true usually costs the one who pushes.
old: If I remove what makes me uncomfortable, I will feel better.
new: Pushing truth out of my life hurts me more than it hurts the truth.
try: Bring back one reminder you pushed away: a talk, a friend, a habit of reading.

title: This is Our way with messengers, and it does not change.
subtitle: A pattern you can count on
then: Ibn Kathir explains this is what Allah {idea}usually does to those who reject His messengers and drive them out{/idea}. He adds that if the Prophet ﷺ were not the Messenger of Mercy, {trap}a punishment never seen before{/trap} would have come. Allah would not punish them while he was among them.
now: Life can feel chaotic, like there are no rules. The verse says there are. {idea}Truth wins in the end, and those who fight it lose.{/idea} That is a pattern you can lean on when you feel outnumbered for doing right.
old: There is no pattern, the powerful just do what they want.
new: Allah has a steady way, and truth always comes out ahead.
try: When you feel alone in doing right this week, remember this verse and keep going.

title: Prayer from midday into night, and the dawn recitation is witnessed.
subtitle: The prayer times, and who is watching at Fajr
then: Ibn Kathir explains this verse points to the times of the five prayers, with the details passed down in the Sunnah. The Prophet ﷺ said the dawn recitation {reward}is witnessed by the angels of the night and the angels of the day{/reward}. They ascend and are asked how they left His servants, and they say: {reward}we came while they were praying and left while they were praying{/reward}.
now: The alarm at 5am. Warm bed, cold floor. It feels like no one would know if you skipped it. {reward}Two groups of angels are gathering right then.{/reward} Picture them reporting: we left them praying.
old: Fajr is just a hard prayer no one notices.
new: Fajr is witnessed, and the angels carry my prayer up to my Lord.
try: Tomorrow, pray Fajr on time and recite a little extra Quran in it.

title: Rise at night, and you may be raised to a praised station.
subtitle: Tahajjud and the station of intercession
then: Asked which prayer is best after the obligatory ones, the Prophet ﷺ said {reward}the night prayer{/reward}. Tahajjud is prayer after sleeping. Ibn 'Abbas said the praised station is {reward}the station of intercession{/reward}, where the Prophet ﷺ will intercede for people on the Day. For the rest of the community, extra prayers can wipe away sins.
now: You wake at 3am anyway, worried about rent or a sick child, and reach for your phone. {idea}Instead, two rak'ahs.{/idea} The house is quiet, the worry has somewhere to go, and you are talking to the One who can fix it.
old: Night prayer is for the very pious, not people like me.
new: Even two short rak'ahs at night are a gift I can give my soul.
try: Tonight, pray two short rak'ahs before you sleep or when you wake in the night.

title: My Lord, let me enter well and leave well, and support me.
subtitle: The dua for every transition

row.title: Allah's help
sub: in the going and the coming

then: Ibn 'Abbas said the Prophet ﷺ was in Makkah and {idea}commanded to emigrate{/idea}, and this verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said the entry was into Madinah, the exit from Makkah. Qatadah said he asked for authority to support the Book of Allah, and that {reward}authority is a mercy that stops the strong from consuming the weak{/reward}.
now: The first day at the new job. Moving cities. Leaving a marriage, or entering one. Starting university far from home. {idea}Every door has an exit and an entry.{/idea} This is the dua for both.
old: A big change is about getting the logistics right.
new: Every exit and entry in my life needs Allah's blessing to be truly good.
try: Memorize this dua and say it before your next big change, even a new week.

title: Truth has come and falsehood has vanished.
subtitle: Falsehood is built to collapse
then: Ibn Mas'ud narrated that when the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah at the Conquest, {trap}there were 360 idols around the Ka'bah{/trap}. He struck them with a stick in his hand, reciting this verse. Ibn Kathir says falsehood {idea}cannot remain or stand firm in the face of truth{/idea}.
now: A lie about you spreads at work. A trend you know is wrong seems to be everywhere. {idea}Falsehood is loud but hollow.{/idea} The verse was recited at the very moment the idols fell. Be patient. Keep standing with what is true.
old: When falsehood is everywhere, truth does not stand a chance.
new: Falsehood is built to vanish, and truth outlasts it every time.
try: Quietly correct one falsehood today, gently, without arguing.

title: The Quran is healing and mercy for those who believe.
subtitle: Same words, different effect
then: Ibn Kathir says the Quran {reward}takes away doubt, hypocrisy, shirk and confusion from the heart{/reward}. It is a mercy through which one gains faith and wisdom. For one who wrongs himself, {trap}it only pushes him further{/trap}. The problem is with the listener, not the Quran.
now: Anxiety at night. A heart full of resentment. A head full of doubt. You open the Quran expecting nothing, read one page slowly, and something settles. {reward}That is the cure working.{/reward}
old: The Quran is for rituals, not for what is going on inside me.
new: The Quran heals what is inside me when I open my heart to it.
try: When you feel low today, read one page of the Quran slowly with its meaning.

title: Blessed, he turns away. Hurt, he despairs.
subtitle: The two moods that pull us from Allah
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {trap}a weakness inherent in man{/trap}, except those Allah protects. With wealth and health, he turns away from worship. With disaster, he thinks nothing good will ever come again. He cites the exception: {reward}those who are patient and do good{/reward}, who get forgiveness and great reward.
now: The raise comes in and you skip prayers for a month. The diagnosis comes and you feel Allah has abandoned you. {idea}Same person, two extremes.{/idea} He was there in both.
old: When things are good I do not need Allah much, and when they are bad He has left me.
new: Allah is with me in ease and hardship, and I can stay steady with Him in both.
try: If today is a good day, thank Allah for it. If it is hard, ask Him for patience.

title: Each acts by his own nature. Your Lord knows who is guided.
subtitle: Your way shows what is inside you
then: Ibn 'Abbas said shakilah means {idea}his inclinations{/idea}. Mujahid said his inclinations and nature, Qatadah said his intentions, Ibn Zayd said his religion. Ibn Kathir reads it as a warning to the idolaters: {trap}everyone will be repaid for their deeds{/trap}, for nothing is hidden from Allah.
now: Your habits tell the story of your heart. What you do when no one is watching, what you spend your evenings on. {idea}Your actions grow from what is inside.{/idea} And only Allah sees the full picture, yours and everyone else's.
old: I can tell exactly who is right and who is wrong around me.
new: My deeds come from what is inside me, and only Allah truly knows who is guided.
try: Look at how you spent last evening. Ask what it says about what you love.

title: The soul belongs to my Lord's affair. Your knowledge is little.
subtitle: Humility before the unknown
then: Ibn Mas'ud narrated that while walking with the Prophet ﷺ, some People of the Book asked him about the soul. He fell silent and {idea}received revelation{/idea}, then recited this verse. 'Ikrimah reported that whatever knowledge you are given {reward}is great if it saves you from the Fire{/reward}, but next to Allah's knowledge it is very little.
now: You read articles on consciousness late at night. Brain scans, theories, podcasts. Still no one can tell you what you actually are. {idea}The verse is honest about that.{/idea} Keep learning, and stay humble about how much you know.
old: Given enough time, humans will understand everything.
new: Some things belong to Allah alone, and my knowledge is a small gift.
try: Next time you learn something new, say alhamdulillah for the little knowledge you have been given.

title: If He willed, He could take back what He revealed.
subtitle: The Quran is a gift that could be withdrawn
then: Ibn Kathir says this verse reminds of the great blessing of the Quran. Ibn Mas'ud said that at the end of time {trap}a wind will come and nothing will be left in a person's mushaf or heart, not even one verse{/trap}, and he recited this verse.
now: The mushaf on your shelf. The app on your phone. The surahs you learned as a child. {idea}You assume they will always be there.{/idea} What you have memorized and lived by is the part that stays with you.
old: The Quran will always be there whenever I get around to it.
new: The Quran is a gift I could lose, so I hold it close now.
try: Review one surah you memorized as a child, so it stays fresh in your heart.

title: It stays only as mercy, and His favor on you is great.
subtitle: Why the Quran is still with us
then: Right after saying He could take it away, Allah says it remains {reward}as a mercy from your Lord{/reward}. Ibn Kathir describes the Quran as {idea}the Book falsehood cannot reach{/idea}, sent by the All-Wise, a bounty on His servant and Messenger ﷺ.
now: You hear a child reciting at the masjid, or a voice on the radio in a taxi. {reward}Every recitation you hear is mercy still flowing.{/reward} It did not have to stay. It stays because He is kind.
old: Having the Quran is just a normal fact of my life.
new: That the Quran is still with me is a daily mercy.
try: Before you read Quran today, pause and thank Allah that it is still in your hands.

title: All humans and jinn together could not produce its like.
subtitle: The open challenge
then: Ibn Kathir says even if all humans and jinn came together and helped one another, {idea}they could never produce anything like it{/idea}. How could the words of created beings be like {idea}the words of the Creator, who has no equal{/idea}?
now: You have read thousands of books, captions, articles, messages. Most you forgot in a day. {idea}This one has been recited daily for over fourteen centuries.{/idea} Next time you read it, notice it is not like anything else you read.
old: The Quran is a great book among many great books.
new: The Quran is the speech of Allah, and nothing written can match it.
try: Read one short surah aloud slowly today and listen to it as Allah's own words.

title: Every kind of example given, yet most refused.
subtitle: When proof is not the problem
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah {idea}furnished them with evidence and definitive proof{/idea} and explained the truth in detail. Despite that, {trap}most people insisted on denying and rejecting it{/trap}.
now: You keep saying you need one more lecture, one more book, one more sign before you change. {idea}You already have plenty.{/idea} Maybe the next step is not more information but one small act.
old: Once I have enough proof, I will change.
new: The proof is already here. What I need is the will to act on it.
try: Pick one thing you already know you should do. Do it today, without waiting for more proof.

title: Make a spring gush from the ground, then we will believe.
subtitle: The list of demands begins
then: Ibn Ishaq narrated that the leaders of Quraysh gathered behind the Ka'bah and sent for the Prophet ﷺ. He came quickly, {reward}hoping they would be guided{/reward}. They offered him wealth, leadership, even kingship. He refused all of it: {idea}Allah has sent me as a messenger, to bring good news and a warning{/idea}. Then the demands began.
now: You tell Allah: give me the job and I will pray on time. Heal my mother and I will wear hijab. Fix my marriage, then I will start reading Quran. {trap}Faith on condition.{/trap} He is not a vending machine. He already gave you the message.
old: If Allah gives me what I ask for, then I will commit.
new: Faith is not a deal I make with Allah after He pays up first.
try: Start one good habit today that you had been saving until Allah gives you something.

title: Or a garden of palms and grapes with rivers flowing.
subtitle: Asking for luxury as proof
then: They told the Prophet ﷺ their land was small and their life hard, and asked him to {trap}move the mountains away and make rivers flow like those of Syria and Iraq{/trap}. He replied: {idea}I was not sent for this{/idea}. If you accept what I brought, it is your good fortune in this world and the next.
now: You judge whether someone's advice is worth hearing by their car, their house, their followers. {trap}A rich person must be right.{/trap} The truth does not need a garden to prove it.
old: Success and wealth are signs that someone is on the right path.
new: Truth stands on its own, with or without a garden around it.
try: Listen today to someone wise who has little money, and take their advice seriously.

title: Or bring the sky down on us, or bring Allah and angels.
subtitle: Demands that dared punishment
then: When they demanded that the sky fall on them, the Prophet ﷺ said: {idea}that is for Allah to decide; if He wills, He will do it{/idea}. One of them said they would never believe until he brought Allah and the angels before them. {trap}When they said this, the Prophet ﷺ got up and left them.{/trap}
now: Some arguments you cannot win, because the other side is not looking for an answer. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ stood up and left.{/idea} You can too, calmly, when a debate online or at dinner becomes mockery.
old: I have to keep arguing until the other person admits I am right.
new: When someone only wants to mock, I can walk away calmly and leave it to Allah.
try: Next time a conversation about faith turns mocking, end it politely and make dua for them.

title: Glory be to my Lord. Am I anything but a human messenger?
subtitle: The humble answer to impossible demands
then: They said even if he climbed into the sky, {trap}we will not believe until you bring down a book we can read{/trap}. They also asked him for palaces of gold, so he would not need to seek provision in the markets like them. His answer begins with {idea}glory be to my Lord{/idea}, then: I am only a human sent as a messenger.
now: People expect you to be perfect because you pray. Or you expect it of your imam, your parents, yourself. {idea}Even the best of creation said: I am a human.{/idea} He was honest about it, and still did his job fully.
